interviewQuestions.question: At a high level, how does a text-to-image model like Stable Diffusion work?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
I'd walk through it as training vs generation, since that's the cleanest way to explain diffusion. In training, you take a real image, repeatedly add small amounts of noise until it's pure static, and train a network to predict the noise added at each step — so it learns to reverse that process, one denoising step at a time.

At generation time, you start from pure random noise instead of a real image, and run the learned denoising step repeatedly, gradually turning static into a coherent image. To make it text-to-image, a text encoder converts the prompt into an embedding that's fed into the denoising network at every single step, steering each step's noise-removal toward an image consistent with the description — that's why prompt wording has such a strong, granular effect on the output.

I'd mention Stable Diffusion specifically runs this whole process in a compressed **latent space** rather than on raw pixels (latent diffusion), decoding to a full image only at the very end, which is what makes it fast enough to run on consumer hardware.

**Testing:** whether you can explain the forward/reverse noise process clearly, and whether you know where and how text conditioning actually enters the pipeline — not just that it "uses AI to make pictures."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Explaining Stable Diffusion end to end

interviewQuestions.question: Why does generating one image with a diffusion model require running the network dozens or hundreds of times, when an LLM generates each token in a single forward pass?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The two are solving genuinely different problems. An LLM generates one discrete token per forward pass because it only needs to compute a probability distribution over a manageable vocabulary and sample from it — cheap, one shot, done for that position. A diffusion model isn't predicting a discrete choice at all; it's trying to turn pure random noise into a coherent image, and that transformation is too large and unconstrained to do correctly in a single step — asking a network to jump directly from static to a finished photorealistic image in one pass produces garbage, because the mapping from arbitrary noise to a specific realistic image is enormously complex and the network has no intermediate structure to anchor on.

Running it as many small, incremental denoising steps instead makes each individual step's job much easier and better-defined: at any given noise level, the network only has to predict and remove a *small* amount of noise, refining a mostly-formed image slightly rather than inventing one from nothing. Each step's output becomes the next step's input, so the image progressively resolves from static into something coherent — which is exactly the same principle that made deep learning's layer-by-layer decomposition work in the first place, just applied along a noise-level axis instead of a network-depth axis.

This is also precisely why diffusion is slower than GANs (a single forward pass) at generation time, and why a large body of research (distillation, fewer-step samplers like DDIM) exists specifically to reduce the step count without losing quality — the many-step process is a real cost, not an incidental implementation detail.

**Testing:** whether you understand why iterative refinement is structurally necessary here, not just "that's how diffusion works."
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Why diffusion needs many steps

interviewQuestions.question: Your team wants a diffusion-based image feature to run in a real-time interactive product (users adjusting a prompt live). What are the actual constraints, and how would you approach hitting a latency budget?
interviewQuestions.answerMarkdown:
The core tension is that diffusion's quality comes specifically from many sequential denoising steps, and real-time interaction wants sub-second or near-instant response — those pull in opposite directions, so I'd frame this explicitly as a quality-vs-latency trade rather than looking for a free lunch. First lever: latent diffusion is close to mandatory here — running the process in a compressed latent space instead of raw pixels cuts the per-step cost by roughly an order of magnitude, and Stable Diffusion already does this by default, so I'd confirm the deployed pipeline actually uses it rather than a pixel-space variant.

Second lever: reduce the number of denoising steps. Naive DDPM-style sampling needs hundreds to thousands of steps, but faster samplers (DDIM, and further distillation-based approaches) can produce comparable quality in as few as 4-20 steps, which is the single biggest lever for hitting an interactive latency budget — I'd benchmark quality degradation at each step count against the product's actual quality bar rather than assuming fewer steps is unacceptable.

Third, infrastructure: batching concurrent user requests on the same GPU, and potentially caching or reusing intermediate latents when a user only tweaks the prompt slightly rather than starting over, if the product interaction pattern supports it. If after all of that the latency still doesn't meet the bar, I'd escalate the real conversation: is a GAN-based generator (single forward pass, much faster, historically lower quality) actually the better product trade-off for this specific interactive use case, even at a quality cost.

**Testing:** whether you treat this as an explicit engineering trade-off with concrete levers (latent space, step count, sampler choice, batching) rather than assuming diffusion can be made real-time for free.
interviewQuestions.subTitle: Diffusion latency in an interactive product
